title: Action Taken Report (ATR): Meaning, Use and How to Follow Up on Your Complaint
seoTitle: Action Taken Report (ATR) – Meaning and How to Follow Up on a Police Complaint
description: What an Action Taken Report means in police and grievance matters, what the BNSS says about informing complainants, and how to follow up.
html:
An Action Taken Report (ATR) is a report in which an authority records what steps it has taken on a complaint or direction. The term is used widely in government grievance systems, vigilance and Lokayukta complaints, court-directed enquiries and police petitions. In a police station context, an ATR (or a "status report") tells the complainant or the court what the police did after the complaint was received.

Where you will meet an ATR

  • Police petitions. When a complaint is given to a police station or a senior officer, the officer may call for an ATR from the station on what action was taken.
  • Courts. The High Court or a Magistrate may ask the police or an authority to file an ATR on the steps taken in compliance with an order.
  • Grievance portals. On central and state grievance portals, the department closes a grievance by uploading an ATR.
  • Vigilance and Lokayukta complaints. The authority forwards the complaint to the department and asks for an ATR.

What a good ATR should contain

  • The reference number of the complaint and the date received.
  • A summary of the allegation being examined.
  • The steps taken: enquiry, statements recorded, documents collected, registration of an FIR or reasons for not registering.
  • The outcome, with reasons, and the date.
  • The name and designation of the officer who prepared it.

What the law says about informing the complainant

Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), the police must inform the informant or victim about the progress of the investigation within ninety days and keep them informed thereafter, including by electronic communication. When a complaint discloses a cognizable offence, the police are expected to register an FIR. For certain offences with punishment of three to seven years, the police may conduct a preliminary enquiry of up to fourteen days with the permission of a senior officer. These provisions help a complainant to ask for a written account of what has been done.

If the police file a closure report saying no offence is made out, the Magistrate must give the informant notice and an opportunity to object, usually through a protest petition. The Supreme Court established this safeguard in Bhagwant Singh v. Commissioner of Police (1985).

How to follow up if you do not get an ATR

  1. Keep the acknowledgement. At a Chennai police station this is generally the receipt for the petition, which is entered in the Community Service Register (CSR). Do not leave without one.
  2. Write to the senior officer. If no action is taken, send a written complaint with a copy of the receipt to the Deputy Commissioner or Commissioner of Police. Under BNSS Section 173(4), you can approach the Superintendent of Police if the station refuses to register an FIR.
  3. Approach the Magistrate. If the police still fail to register an FIR, you can apply to the Magistrate under Section 175(3) of the BNSS, with an affidavit, to direct registration and investigation.
  4. Use the Right to Information Act. Ask for the file notings or status of the complaint, subject to exemptions.
  5. Writ or Section 528 petition. In appropriate cases, the High Court can direct the police to act or to file a report.

Frequently asked questions

Is an ATR the same as a charge sheet?

No. A charge sheet, or final report, is the police report filed in court after investigation. An ATR is a record of the action taken on a complaint or direction.

Can I get a copy of the ATR?

In many cases, yes. If the ATR was prepared in response to your complaint, you can ask for it, and the Right to Information Act is available where it is denied.

What if the police say no offence is made out?

Ask for the reasons in writing. You can approach senior officers, the Magistrate or the High Court.

Does the police have to register an FIR on every complaint?

For a cognizable offence, yes, following Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2014), subject to a limited preliminary enquiry in specified categories.

Who prepares an ATR on a court order?

The authority that was directed, such as the police or the concerned department, and the court may ask for it to be sworn.

title: How to Appeal a Maintenance Order Under the BNSS: Step by Step
seoTitle: Appeal Against a Maintenance Order Under BNSS – Step-by-Step Guide
description: Where and how to challenge a maintenance order passed under Section 144 BNSS (earlier Section 125 CrPC): appeal, revision, limitation, grounds and interim stay.
html:
An order granting or refusing maintenance under Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which replaced Section 125 of the CrPC, can be challenged. The correct remedy depends on which court passed the order and whether the order is final or interim. This guide walks through the steps for a person who wishes to challenge an order, whether as the paying spouse or as the claimant.

Step 1: Identify the order and the court

  • Final order of a Family Court. An appeal lies to the High Court under Section 19 of the Family Courts Act, 1984, ordinarily within thirty days of the order.
  • Order of a Magistrate (where there is no Family Court). A revision lies to the Sessions Court or the High Court under the revision provisions of the BNSS (Section 438 onwards).
  • Interim maintenance order. The Family Courts Act does not allow an appeal against an interim order, so the usual route is a revision or a petition under the High Court's inherent power (Section 528 BNSS) in an appropriate case.

Step 2: Check limitation

For a Family Court appeal, the period is thirty days from the date of the order. If you are late, apply to condone the delay, supported by an affidavit explaining the reason. Courts allow delay for good reason but do not do so automatically.

Step 3: Obtain the records

Get a certified copy of the order, the petition, the counter, the evidence and any interim orders. Check what income, assets and expenses the court considered.

Step 4: Identify the grounds

Typical grounds in a maintenance appeal include:

  • the court misjudged the husband's income or ignored his liabilities;
  • the court ignored the wife's income or capacity to earn, or other relevant material;
  • the amount is disproportionate to the evidence;
  • the court did not follow the Supreme Court's guidance requiring disclosure of income and assets by affidavit (Rajnesh v. Neha, 2020);
  • there is a legal bar, for example where the claimant is living in adultery or where parties are living separately by mutual consent without sufficient reason;
  • the order for arrears or the date from which maintenance is payable is wrong.

For a claimant who is dissatisfied, the grounds usually relate to an inadequate amount, the failure to consider lifestyle, or the date from which maintenance starts.

Step 5: Draft and file the appeal or revision

Prepare the memorandum of appeal or the revision petition, with a list of dates, grounds and prayer. Attach the certified copy of the order, the key documents and an affidavit. File it in the High Court (or the Sessions Court for revision, where applicable) along with court fee and vakalatnama.

Step 6: Ask for a stay if needed

If the order requires immediate payment, you can apply for stay or suspension of the order. Courts often require the appellant to deposit a part of the arrears or continue paying an interim amount as a condition. A stay is not automatic.

Step 7: Follow the hearing and comply meanwhile

Until the High Court stays or modifies the order, it remains enforceable. Non-payment can lead to a warrant for recovery and, in some cases, imprisonment of up to one month for each month of default. Keep paying whatever is directed and keep proof of every payment.

Frequently asked questions

Can a maintenance order be modified later without an appeal?

Yes. If circumstances change, either party can apply to the same court to alter the allowance.

Is there a time limit to file a revision?

Ninety days is generally taken as the period for a revision to the High Court, subject to condonation of delay.

Will the High Court re-hear the whole evidence?

In an appeal, it can examine the record afresh. In revision, its review is more limited to legality and propriety.

What if my spouse has hidden income?

The court can draw conclusions from lifestyle, bank records and the failure to disclose. The disclosure affidavit makes concealment risky.

Can I appeal if maintenance was refused?

Yes, the claimant has the same right of appeal or revision.

title: Extramarital Affairs and the Law in India: Adultery, Divorce and Maintenance
seoTitle: Extramarital Affairs and the Law in India – Divorce, Maintenance and Evidence
description: Adultery is no longer a crime in India, but an affair can still affect divorce, maintenance and custody. What evidence courts accept.
html:
Adultery is no longer a crime in India. In Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court struck down Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 does not contain an offence of adultery. However, an extramarital affair continues to matter in civil and family law: it can be a ground for divorce, can influence maintenance and can be relevant in custody and in other proceedings.

Adultery as a ground for divorce

  • Under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, a spouse can seek divorce if the other has had voluntary sexual intercourse with a person other than the spouse after the marriage.
  • The Special Marriage Act, 1954 and personal laws of other communities provide similar grounds in their own terms.
  • A spouse can also rely on cruelty, which in some cases is established by a spouse's conduct outside the marriage, depending on its effect on the other spouse.

The burden is on the spouse who alleges adultery, and the court needs reliable proof. Suspicion is not enough.

Effect on maintenance

A wife who is living in adultery is not entitled to maintenance under Section 144 of the BNSS (earlier Section 125 CrPC), and the husband may use this ground to oppose the claim, though it must be proved. In proceedings under personal laws, the conduct of the parties is also considered. A husband's own affair does not disqualify him from paying maintenance, and the court may consider his conduct while deciding custody and the financial settlement.

Custody and children

Courts decide custody on the welfare of the child. An extramarital relationship by a parent is not by itself a bar to custody, but conduct that harms the child's welfare, such as neglect or exposure to unsuitable environments, can matter.

Other legal issues linked to affairs

  • Bigamy. A second marriage during the subsistence of the first is an offence (Section 82 of the BNS), independent of adultery.
  • Cheating or harassment. If a person is deceived into a relationship, or if threats, stalking or blackmail occur, criminal laws on those offences apply.
  • Defamation. Public allegations of an affair can lead to defamation claims.
  • Privacy. Secretly recording calls, accessing a spouse's phone or placing tracking tools can raise privacy and cyber law issues.

What evidence courts accept

  • Photographs, messages and call records, if lawfully obtained and properly proved. Electronic evidence requires a certificate under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (earlier Section 65B of the Evidence Act).
  • Hotel records, travel records and witness testimony.
  • Admissions made by the spouse.

Evidence obtained through illegal access to accounts or devices can create problems for the person who collected it.

Practical steps

  1. Do not confront or threaten. Threats can create criminal liability for you.
  2. Preserve information but avoid hacking or unlawful surveillance.
  3. Consider mediation or counselling, which courts often encourage before a divorce.
  4. Take advice on financial and custody consequences before filing or responding.

Frequently asked questions

Can my spouse file a criminal case against the other person?

Not for adultery. Other offences such as cheating, stalking or blackmail can still be reported.

Can I get divorce on the ground of my spouse's affair?

Yes, if you can prove it. The petition is filed in the Family Court with the evidence.

Does an affair affect child custody?

It is only one factor. The court's focus is the child's welfare.

Can I record my spouse's phone calls?

Recording without consent can violate privacy and may not be admissible. Seek legal advice before doing so.

Is adultery a ground for divorce for both husband and wife?

Yes, the ground is available to either spouse under the main marriage laws.

title: Contempt of Court Notice Format: Demand Notice and Contempt Petition
seoTitle: Contempt of Court Notice Format – Demand Notice and Petition Outline
description: Format of a notice demanding compliance with a court order, a contempt petition outline for the Madras High Court, and replying to a show-cause notice.
html:
When a person or authority does not comply with a court order, the party who obtained the order can take two steps: first, send a notice demanding compliance, and then, if there is no response, file a contempt petition in the court. This page gives the usual format of both documents, and explains how to respond if you receive a show-cause notice. The contempt law is the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, read with Articles 129 and 215 of the Constitution.

A notice before filing is advisable, not mandatory

The Act does not require a notice before a contempt petition, but courts like to see that the other side was made aware of the order and given a reasonable chance to comply. A notice also helps to prove that the disobedience was wilful.

Format of a demand notice

Heading: "Notice demanding compliance with the order dated ___ passed by the Hon'ble High Court of Madras in W.P. / C.S. / Crl.O.P. No. ___ of ___."

Sent to: the person or officer responsible for compliance, at the official address, by registered post, speed post and email, with proof of delivery.

Body:

  1. Introduction. State who you are and in which case the order was passed.
  2. The order. Quote the operative part of the order and attach a certified copy.
  3. Knowledge. State that the order was communicated or served on a specified date.
  4. Non-compliance. Describe exactly what has not been done and the date by which it was required.
  5. Demand. Ask for compliance within a stated period, such as seven or ten days.
  6. Consequence. State that if there is no compliance, contempt proceedings will be filed, and costs will be claimed.
  7. Signature. Signed by the party or the advocate.

Outline of a civil contempt petition in the Madras High Court

  1. Cause title: "In the High Court of Judicature at Madras, Contempt Petition (Civil) No. ___ of 2026, in W.P. No. ___ of ___."
  2. Heading: "Petition filed under Sections 11 and 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 and Article 215 of the Constitution of India to punish the respondent for wilful disobedience of the order dated ___."
  3. Affidavit and facts: the case history, the order, the date of service, the steps taken to obtain compliance, and why non-compliance is wilful.
  4. Grounds: the order was clear; the respondent knew of it; there was no impossibility; the respondent had the capacity to comply; and the delay is deliberate.
  5. Prayer: to take action against the respondent for contempt and to direct compliance.
  6. Annexures: certified copy of the order, proof of service, the demand notice and the reply, if any.

Remember the one-year limitation in Section 20 of the Act, counted from the date of the alleged contempt.

If you receive a show-cause notice

  • Read the order said to be violated and understand its exact terms.
  • File a detailed response with an affidavit on what was done and when. If compliance has been completed, attach proof.
  • Explain any inability to comply, such as an unclear direction, a pending appeal or a stay order. Wilfulness is essential for contempt.
  • Consider a sincere apology where there was a lapse. Courts may accept a bona fide apology.
  • Appear on the date given. Failing to appear can lead to a coercive process.

Frequently asked questions

Is a notice required before filing a contempt petition?

No, but it is good practice, and courts often expect that the other side was given an opportunity to comply.

Who is liable in the case of a government department?

The officer responsible for compliance may be called to appear. Courts focus on the officer who had the duty to implement the order.

Can I file a contempt petition if there is an appeal pending?

Yes, unless the order has been stayed. A stay or the pendency of an appeal without stay does not suspend the order.

What is the difference between contempt and execution?

Execution enforces the decree by process of the court. Contempt punishes disobedience to maintain the authority of the court.

What punishment can follow?

Simple imprisonment up to six months, a fine up to ₹2,000, or both, unless the court accepts an apology.

title: How Long Does a Criminal Trial Take in India? Stages and Delays Explained
seoTitle: How Long Does a Criminal Trial Take in India? Stages, Delays and Timelines
description: Stages of a criminal trial in India from FIR to judgment, what causes delay, the speedy trial right and BNSS timelines. No two cases take equal time.
html:
There is no fixed duration for a criminal trial in India. A simple summons case before a Magistrate may finish in months, while a serious Sessions Court trial with many witnesses can take several years. The actual time depends on the offence, the number of accused and witnesses, the court's workload and whether the case is delayed by adjournments or higher court proceedings. This page explains the stages so that you can understand where time is spent.

Stages of a typical criminal case

  1. Complaint and FIR. The case begins with an FIR or a private complaint.
  2. Investigation. The police collect evidence, record statements and make arrests. A charge sheet must be filed within 60 or 90 days of the start of custody for the accused to be denied default bail, depending on the offence.
  3. Cognizance and supply of documents. The court takes cognizance of the charge sheet and the accused receives copies of the documents.
  4. Committal (Sessions cases). For offences triable only by the Sessions Court, the Magistrate commits the case.
  5. Framing of charges. After hearing both sides, the court frames charges or discharges the accused.
  6. Prosecution evidence. Witnesses are examined and cross-examined. This is usually the longest stage.
  7. Statement of the accused. The accused is asked to explain the incriminating evidence.
  8. Defence evidence. The defence may lead evidence, though it is not obliged to.
  9. Final arguments. Both sides argue and file written submissions.
  10. Judgment. The court acquits or convicts. If convicted, there is a hearing on sentence.
  11. Appeal or revision. The decision can be challenged in a higher court.

Why trials take time

  • Witnesses not appearing or being untraceable, so that dates are repeatedly adjourned.
  • Large numbers of accused and witnesses, especially in conspiracy, financial and organised crime cases.
  • Forensic and expert reports that are delayed.
  • Court workload and vacancies, which cause long gaps between hearings.
  • Interim proceedings, such as petitions for quashing, transfer or bail in higher courts.
  • Absence of the accused or counsel, which requires fresh dates and processes.

What the law says about speed

The right to a speedy trial is part of Article 21 of the Constitution, recognised in decisions such as Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979). The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 also introduces timelines for several steps, limits on adjournments and provision for electronic proceedings. Special laws such as POCSO set targets for trial completion. These timelines guide the courts but are not always met in practice.

Protection for undertrial prisoners

A person detained during the trial has some legal protection against prolonged custody:

  • Default bail if the investigation is not completed within the statutory time.
  • Release after serving a part of the maximum sentence. Section 479 of the BNSS allows an undertrial who has served one-third of the maximum sentence (if a first-time offender) or one-half (in other cases) to be released on bond. It does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment, or where several cases are pending against the person.
  • Bail on the ground of delay, which courts have granted where the trial is unreasonably prolonged.

What you can do to avoid avoidable delay

  • Attend every hearing, and keep your advocate informed of changes of address.
  • Provide documents and witness details promptly.
  • Avoid unnecessary adjournments; courts increasingly record reasons for them.
  • Consider compounding or settlement, if the offence permits.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get a case closed faster by pleading guilty?

A plea of guilty is a serious decision with legal consequences, and the court may still examine whether it is voluntary. Take advice before doing so.

How long does a cheque bounce case take?

Section 138 cases are meant to be tried summarily, but they often take longer than intended.

Does a High Court stay stop the trial?

A stay of the trial proceedings pauses it until the High Court decides the petition.

Is there a time limit for a trial to end?

Not in general. Some special laws set targets, and the Constitution protects the right to a speedy trial.

Can an accused ask for a speedy trial?

Yes. An application for a speedy trial, or a petition in the High Court, can be made where delay is causing prejudice.

title: Traffic Challan Cases in Chennai: Court Procedure, Fines and How to Resolve Them
seoTitle: Traffic Challan Court Cases in Chennai – Procedure, Fines and Lok Adalat
description: What happens if a traffic challan goes to court in Chennai, how e-challans and court challans differ, how to pay or contest them, and when a lawyer helps.
html:
A traffic challan in Chennai is either an e-challan that can be paid online, or a court challan that requires you to appear before a Magistrate. Which one you get depends on the offence. Minor violations such as helmet or signal offences are usually settled by paying a fine, while serious offences, such as drunk driving, dangerous driving or driving without a licence, can require a court appearance.

Types of traffic challans

| Type | Usual cases | What you do | |---|---|---| | Spot or e-challan | Helmet, seat belt, signal jumping, parking, speeding captured on camera | Pay online or at the designated counters within the stated period | | Court challan | Drunk driving, driving without licence or insurance, rash driving, unpaid or contested challans | Appear before the Metropolitan Magistrate on the date given |

How to check and pay an e-challan

  • Use the Parivahan portal or the official Chennai traffic police e-challan service, with the vehicle number or challan number.
  • Pay within the stated period to avoid it being sent to the court.
  • Keep the payment receipt, since it is the proof that the matter is closed.

If a challan is unpaid, the matter can be forwarded to the court, and you may receive a summons or notice. Ignoring it can lead to a warrant and additional trouble when you renew your licence or sell the vehicle.

What happens in the court

  1. Appearance. You appear on the date given. The court reads the allegation to you.
  2. Plea. You may plead guilty and pay the fine, or contest the charge.
  3. Evidence. If you contest, the police witness is examined, and you can cross-examine and lead your own evidence.
  4. Order. The Magistrate imposes the fine or other penalty, or acquits you.

Fines depend on the offence as set out in the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and its 2019 amendments. For some offences, the court can also order suspension of the licence.

Settling cases through compounding and Lok Adalat

Many minor traffic offences can be compounded, meaning the offender pays a prescribed amount and the case ends, without a trial. Courts also hold Lok Adalats, where pending and pre-litigation traffic challans can be settled, often with a reduced fine. Check the eCourts services and the District Legal Services Authority for the dates of such events in Chennai.

When to consider a lawyer

  • The challan is for a serious offence with possible imprisonment or licence suspension.
  • You dispute the facts, such as the vehicle number, identity, speed or location.
  • Several challans have accumulated and you need to resolve them together.
  • Your licence or vehicle has been impounded, and you need to recover it.

Practical tips

  • Always take a receipt for any document or licence handed over to the police.
  • Do not ignore a notice, because the consequences can multiply.
  • Do not pay agents or offer money. Offering a bribe is a separate offence.
  • Check that the vehicle number and the location in the challan are correct.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to go to court for every challan?

No. Most e-challans can be paid online. A court appearance is needed when the challan is a court challan or has been referred to court.

Can my licence be suspended for traffic challans?

For certain offences and for repeated violations, the authorities or the court can suspend or disqualify a licence.

What if I was not driving the vehicle?

Inform the court or the authority and provide details of who was driving. The registered owner may be asked to explain.

Is there a time limit to pay?

A period is stated in the challan. After it expires, additional steps can follow.

Can I contest an e-challan generated by camera?

Yes, if there is a mistake. Follow the dispute procedure on the portal, or raise it in court.

title: How to Cross-Examine the Complainant in a Section 138 NI Act Trial
seoTitle: Cross-Examining the Complainant in a Section 138 Cheque Bounce Trial
description: Key areas of cross-examination in a cheque bounce trial: the presumptions, legally enforceable debt, documents, notice and authority of the complainant.
html:
In a cheque bounce trial under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the case often turns on the cross-examination of the complainant. The law starts with two presumptions in the complainant's favour: that the cheque was issued for a debt or liability (Section 139) and that a negotiable instrument was made for consideration (Section 118). The accused's task is to raise a probable defence that shakes these presumptions, and the cross-examination is the main tool for doing so. This page is for general understanding; actual cross-examination is a skill exercised by an advocate in court.

How the trial is structured

  • Section 138 cases follow a summary trial procedure (Section 143), intended to be quick.
  • The complainant's evidence is given by affidavit (Section 145), and the accused can apply to cross-examine the complainant on it.
  • After the complainant's evidence, the court records the statement of the accused, and the accused may lead evidence.

The burden and the standard

The Supreme Court has held that the presumption under Section 139 includes the existence of a legally enforceable debt (Rangappa v. Mohan, 2010). The accused does not have to prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt. It is enough to show, on the preponderance of probabilities, that the existence of the debt is improbable, which can be done through the complainant's own evidence and documents (Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa, 2019). Even a blank signed cheque voluntarily handed over can attract the presumption (Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar, 2019).

Areas commonly explored in cross-examination

  1. The alleged debt. The date, the amount, the reason for the loan and the circumstances. Vague or shifting answers on these points can weaken the claim.
  2. Capacity to lend. The complainant's source of funds, bank statements and income tax returns. In larger cash transactions, questions on compliance with income tax rules on cash loans may arise.
  3. Documents. Whether any promissory note, receipt, ledger entry or message supports the loan, and whether the documents are consistent with the complaint.
  4. The cheque. Who filled in the amount, date and name, and whether the handwriting differs from the signature. Whether the cheque was given as security.
  5. Presentation and dishonour. The dates of presentation, the return memo and the reason for dishonour.
  6. The legal notice. Whether the notice was sent within thirty days of receiving the bank memo, whether it demanded the correct amount and whether it was properly served.
  7. The complaint timeline. Whether the complaint was filed within one month after the fifteen-day payment period.
  8. Authority of the person giving evidence. If a power of attorney holder deposes, whether they have personal knowledge of the transaction (A.C. Narayanan v. State of Maharashtra, 2014).
  9. Inconsistencies between the complaint, the legal notice, the affidavit and the oral evidence.

Points to remember

  • Cross-examination should be precise and purposeful, avoiding questions that allow the complainant to fill gaps in the case.
  • The accused's own statement under the code of criminal procedure is not on oath, but the accused should not make admissions that harm the defence.
  • A rebuttal can also come from the accused's evidence or documents, so the cross-examination should be planned with the defence evidence.
  • If convicted, the accused who appeals must deposit at least twenty per cent of the compensation under Section 148, so planning the defence early is important.

Frequently asked questions

Can the accused avoid cross-examination?

No. It is the accused's main opportunity to challenge the complainant's case.

What if the accused admits signing the cheque?

Admitting the signature supports the presumption. The defence then focuses on showing there was no legally enforceable debt.

Does the complainant need to show the loan in the income tax return?

It is a relevant factor in testing the complainant's case, though not conclusive by itself.

How many questions can be asked?

There is no fixed number, but the court controls irrelevant or repetitive questions.

Can the case be settled during the trial?

Yes. Section 147 allows the offence to be compounded.

title: How Long Does a Forgery Case Take to Resolve in India?
seoTitle: How Long Does a Forgery Case Take? Stages, Experts and Delays in India
description: Stages of a forgery case under the BNS, why handwriting and forensic reports cause delay, what affects the timeline and how a case can end sooner.
html:
There is no standard duration for a forgery case in India. Many cases take several years from the FIR to a final judgment, mostly because of the forensic examination of the disputed document and the usual delays of the criminal justice system. This page explains the stages and the factors that make a forgery case shorter or longer, without promising any timeline.

What forgery means in law

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), the chapter on offences relating to documents (Sections 335 to 342, replacing Sections 463 to 477A of the IPC) covers:

  • making a false document or false electronic record with intent to cause damage, support a claim or commit fraud;
  • forgery, which is the making of a false document with intent to cause damage or injury, or to support a claim, or to commit fraud;
  • forgery of a valuable security or a will, which carries heavier punishment;
  • possessing a forged document, and using it as genuine; and
  • forging a seal or a record of a court or public register.

Forgery is frequently charged together with cheating and criminal conspiracy, especially in property and loan matters.

Stages of a forgery case

  1. Complaint or FIR. Property, banking and employment disputes are the commonest sources.
  2. Investigation. The police collect the disputed documents, admitted writings or signatures, bank records and registrar records.
  3. Forensic examination. The disputed signature or writing is compared with specimen and admitted writings by a handwriting expert or a government forensic laboratory, and the report is received. This stage is often the main cause of delay.
  4. Charge sheet and cognizance. The final report is filed and the court takes cognizance.
  5. Charges and trial. Prosecution witnesses, including the complainant, officials and the expert, are examined.
  6. Judgment and appeal. The accused is acquitted or convicted, and appeals follow.

What affects the time taken

  • Backlog in forensic laboratories and delay in getting the expert's opinion.
  • Number of documents and accused. Multiple documents and several accused increase the number of witnesses.
  • Availability of original documents. Missing or damaged originals create further disputes.
  • Parallel civil proceedings. Title or ownership suits on the same property can proceed alongside, although a criminal case is not automatically stopped by the civil case.
  • Challenges in the High Court. Petitions to quash the FIR, or transfers, can add time.
  • Absence of witnesses or the accused, resulting in adjournments.

Ways in which a case may end sooner

  • Quashing. Where the dispute is essentially civil, or the allegations do not make out forgery, the High Court may quash the FIR under Section 528 of the BNSS.
  • Discharge. The court may discharge the accused if the material does not support the charge.
  • Settlement. Offences of forgery are not compoundable in general, but a genuine settlement of a private dispute can support a quashing petition, depending on the facts and the offence.

What a person facing a forgery allegation should do

  1. Do not destroy or alter any document.
  2. Collect the originals and copies of the documents, including those showing the source of your signatures and the transaction history.
  3. Seek advice before giving specimen handwriting or signatures, as these are used for comparison.
  4. Consider anticipatory bail if arrest is likely.
  5. Explore whether the dispute is civil, since courts do not allow criminal law to be used merely to pressure a party in a civil matter.

Frequently asked questions

Is forgery a bailable offence?

It depends on the section. Forgery for the purpose of cheating or of valuable securities is generally non-bailable, though bail is commonly considered.

Can I be forced to give a handwriting sample?

A Magistrate can direct a person to give specimen writing or signature for comparison, and refusal can lead to adverse consequences.

How reliable is a handwriting expert's opinion?

It is only an opinion, and courts need corroboration and look at the reasons given. It is often tested through cross-examination.

Can a civil case and a forgery case go on together?

Yes. The standards of proof differ, and one does not automatically stop the other.

Does a forgery conviction lead to imprisonment?

It can, depending on the section, with terms ranging up to life imprisonment for forgery of certain valuable securities.

title: Lawyer Fees in a 498A Dowry Harassment Case: What Affects the Cost
seoTitle: Lawyer Fees in a 498A Dowry Harassment Case – What Affects the Cost
description: What determines advocate fees in a 498A (BNS 85) dowry harassment case: stage, courts, number of hearings, settlement, legal aid and Bar Council rules on fees.
html:
There is no fixed fee for a 498A (now Section 85 and 86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) dowry harassment case. Advocates set their fees individually, and the total cost depends on what stage the case is at and how long it runs. This page explains the factors so that you can plan and ask the right questions. It deliberately gives no amounts, because published figures for a legal matter would mislead.

Why costs vary so much

A 498A case rarely consists of a single step. A family may need several proceedings over a number of years:

| Stage | Typical work involved | |---|---| | Before arrest | Anticipatory bail petition, representation to the police, reply to notices | | After FIR | Regular bail, quashing petition in the High Court, if grounds exist | | Investigation | Appearance before the police, joint enquiry in the Mediation Centre, documentation | | Trial | Charge stage, evidence of several witnesses, cross-examination, final arguments | | Appeal | Appeal or revision against conviction or acquittal | | Connected cases | Divorce, maintenance, domestic violence and custody proceedings |

Factors that influence the fee

  • Number of accused persons and whether the family needs separate representation.
  • Court and place. Appearances in the Magistrate court, Sessions Court, High Court or outside Chennai will differ.
  • Length of the trial, which depends on the number of witnesses and adjournments.
  • Parallel proceedings, since the marriage dispute often includes matters in the Family Court.
  • Seniority of counsel and the size of the team.
  • Mediation and settlement. Genuine settlements can reduce the overall cost but still require drafting and appearances.

Bar Council rules and fairness

An advocate may not charge a fee that depends on the result of the case or promise a particular outcome. A fee may be fixed by stage or by appearance, but it should be disclosed and agreed in advance. You are entitled to ask for a receipt for every payment, and to be told clearly how fees apply to adjournments and later stages.

Tips for managing cost

  1. Ask for a written fee agreement that states what the fee covers (for example, an anticipatory bail petition) and what is excluded.
  2. Ask how fees apply across stages, so that you are not surprised later.
  3. Plan for related expenses, such as court fees, certified copies, travel and translations.
  4. Keep your documents organised so that your advocate's time is used well.
  5. Discuss settlement early, where it is a realistic option.

Legal aid

If you cannot afford a lawyer, free legal aid is available to women and to persons below a specified income under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. A person in custody can ask the Magistrate for a legal aid advocate, and the District Legal Services Authority in Chennai can be approached directly.

Frequently asked questions

Is a 498A case a one-time fee?

Usually not. The work extends over several stages, and fees are commonly agreed by stage.

Does a higher fee improve the outcome?

No. The result depends on law and evidence, and no advocate can guarantee it.

Will a settlement end the fees?

Settlement reduces ongoing costs but may still involve drafting, mediation and a High Court petition for quashing.

Can the wife claim litigation costs?

In maintenance and matrimonial proceedings, courts can direct the husband to pay litigation expenses in appropriate cases.

Are there free alternatives to a private lawyer?

Yes, through legal aid for those who qualify, and through mediation centres attached to courts.

title: How to Choose a Cheque Bounce Lawyer in Chennai (Section 138 NI Act)
seoTitle: Choosing a Cheque Bounce Lawyer in Chennai – Section 138 Timelines and Checklist
description: A checklist for choosing a lawyer for a Section 138 cheque bounce case in Chennai, with the legal timelines, penalties and settlement options.
html:
A cheque bounce case under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 depends heavily on strict timelines. A missed deadline can end a complaint, so the lawyer you choose should be precise about dates and procedure. This page sets out the legal timeline and a practical checklist, without ranking any lawyer, since quality depends on the facts of your case.

The statutory timeline

| Step | Time limit | |---|---| | Presenting the cheque to the bank | Within the validity of the cheque, ordinarily three months from the date on it | | Sending the legal notice to the drawer | Within 30 days of receiving the bank's return memo | | Drawer's time to pay | 15 days from receipt of the notice | | Filing the complaint in court | Within one month after the 15 days expire |

The court can condone a delay in filing the complaint if sufficient cause is shown, but the notice period is strict.

Where to file

Under Section 142(2), as amended in 2015, the complaint is filed in the court within whose jurisdiction the payee's bank branch where the cheque was deposited for collection is situated. For an account maintained in Chennai, the Metropolitan Magistrate courts in Chennai are the usual forum, though facts differ.

Penalty and related powers

  • Imprisonment up to two years, or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.
  • Interim compensation of up to twenty per cent of the cheque amount can be ordered at the start of the trial (Section 143A), and the accused who appeals a conviction must deposit at least twenty per cent (Section 148).
  • The offence can be compounded by settlement at any stage (Section 147).

Checklist for choosing a lawyer

  1. Experience in the right court. Ask whether they regularly handle Section 138 trials and the relevant procedure in the Magistrate courts.
  2. Command of the timelines. A good lawyer will tell you the deadlines for your case on the first meeting, in writing.
  3. Clear advice for your side. The advice differs depending on whether you are the complainant or the accused.
  4. Document review. They should ask for the cheque, the return memo, the notice, the postal proof and the underlying agreement.
  5. Honest about the outcome. Avoid anyone who guarantees a result.
  6. Written fee agreement. It should state the stages covered and any extra charges, and you should get receipts.
  7. Communication. Do you get regular updates and copies of the filings?
  8. Settlement approach. They should explain compounding and negotiation, not only litigation.

If you are the complainant

  • Keep the original cheque and the bank return memo.
  • Send the notice to the correct address by a traceable method, and keep proof.
  • Make sure the notice demands the correct amount.
  • Be ready with proof of the underlying transaction.

If you are the accused

  • Do not ignore the notice. Reply within the time and explain your position.
  • Preserve documents showing payments made, disputes or the absence of a legally enforceable debt.
  • Consider a settlement early, since the case can be compounded.

Frequently asked questions

Can I file a cheque bounce case if the cheque was post-dated?

Yes, once the cheque is presented within its validity and is dishonoured, the process starts from the bank's return memo.

Is a cheque dishonoured for "account closed" covered by Section 138?

Yes. Dishonour for insufficient funds or because the amount exceeds the arrangement are covered, and closed accounts are also generally treated as covered.

Can a company be prosecuted?

Yes, along with persons in charge of its business at the time (Section 141).

Can the case be filed online?

Some courts accept e-filing, which depends on the court's procedure. Ask your lawyer.

How long does the case take?

It is meant to be summary, but it often takes longer than intended. See the cross-examination guide for how trials proceed.

title: Quashing an FIR vs Quashing a Charge Sheet: What Is the Difference?
seoTitle: Quashing an FIR vs Quashing a Charge Sheet – Difference, Grounds and Stage
description: How quashing an FIR differs from quashing a charge sheet: the stage, the High Court test, the Bhajan Lal categories and alternatives like discharge.
html:
Quashing an FIR and quashing a charge sheet use the same legal power, but at different stages and with a slightly different focus. An FIR is the first information that starts the investigation. A charge sheet is the police report filed after the investigation, listing the evidence and the persons the police propose to prosecute. The High Court can quash either (or the entire proceeding pending in court) under its inherent power, Section 482 of the CrPC, now Section 528 of the BNSS.

At a glance

| Point | Quashing an FIR | Quashing a charge sheet / pending case | |---|---|---| | Stage | Early, during investigation | After the police report, when the court has taken cognizance | | What the court looks at | The allegations in the FIR on their face | The FIR together with the material collected in the charge sheet | | Main question | Do the allegations disclose a cognizable offence at all? | Does the material, taken as it stands, make out an offence? | | Interference | Sparingly. The High Court rarely stops a genuine investigation | Slightly wider, because the material is on record, but no "mini-trial" | | Alternative at trial level | None; the High Court is the usual remedy | Application for discharge before the trial court |

The test the High Court applies

The Supreme Court's decision in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992) lists situations where the power may be used. In summary, the High Court may quash where:

  1. the allegations, even if accepted as true, do not disclose any offence;
  2. the allegations do not disclose a cognizable offence that justifies a police investigation;
  3. the allegations and the evidence do not make out the offence alleged;
  4. the offence is non-cognizable and the police investigated without the Magistrate's order;
  5. the allegations are absurd or inherently improbable;
  6. there is an express legal bar to the proceeding; or
  7. the proceeding is manifestly mala fide, started with an ulterior motive or to settle a private grudge.

The court uses this power sparingly, and it does not weigh evidence as a trial court would. Disputed questions of fact are normally left for the trial.

Quashing the FIR

A petition at this stage argues that, on the face of the FIR, no offence is made out, or the dispute is civil in nature, or the complaint is an abuse of process. The High Court may call for a report, hear the Public Prosecutor and sometimes direct "no coercive steps" while the petition is pending.

Quashing the charge sheet or the case

Once the investigation is complete, the petition can rely on the charge sheet's own material, for example by showing that the statements and documents do not support the offence charged. The court may also consider that a trial court discharge application is the better first step, because the trial court can evaluate the material on the legal standard for framing charges.

Choosing between them

  • If the FIR is plainly defective, or the case is a disguised civil dispute, the earlier the challenge the better.
  • If the investigation is complete and the material is weak, the discharge route and a quashing petition may both be possible.
  • If the parties have settled, a petition on compromise may be considered, depending on the offence.

Frequently asked questions

Can I quash an FIR after a charge sheet is filed?

Yes. The petition then seeks to quash the FIR and the proceedings following it.

Does the High Court stay the investigation?

Not usually. Courts are cautious about stopping an investigation, though they may restrain arrest in suitable cases.

Is quashing a final end to the case?

Yes, if the High Court quashes the proceedings. The State can appeal to the Supreme Court.

Where is a quashing petition filed in Tamil Nadu?

In the Madras High Court (or the Madurai Bench, depending on territorial jurisdiction), as a Criminal Original Petition.

Is quashing available for all offences?

The power is wide, but the court uses it carefully, particularly for serious offences.

title: FIR Quashing in the Madras High Court: Grounds, Procedure and What to Expect
seoTitle: FIR Quashing in the Madras High Court – Grounds, Procedure and Process
description: A practical overview of challenging an FIR in the Madras High Court: grounds, the Crl.O.P. procedure, interim relief and what happens at the hearing.
html:
If an FIR has been registered against you, and it discloses no offence or is an abuse of process, you can ask the Madras High Court to quash it. The petition is filed under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (earlier Section 482 of the CrPC), which preserves the High Court's inherent power to prevent abuse of process and secure the ends of justice. This page gives a practical overview of the grounds, the process and what to expect.

Grounds on which FIRs are challenged

  • The facts in the FIR, taken as true, do not constitute the offence alleged.
  • The matter is a civil or commercial dispute that has been given a criminal colour, such as a payment dispute presented as cheating.
  • The complaint is mala fide, motivated by personal enmity or to pressure a party.
  • The FIR is delayed without explanation and is inherently improbable.
  • There is a legal bar to the proceeding, such as the lack of a required sanction or complaint by a competent authority.
  • The parties have settled a private dispute (see the separate article on compromise-based quashing).
  • The same allegations have already been investigated and closed, and a fresh FIR is an abuse.

How the petition is filed

  1. Draft the petition as a Criminal Original Petition (Crl.O.P.) under Section 528 BNSS, with the facts, the legal grounds and the prayer to quash the FIR (and any consequential proceedings).
  2. Attach documents: the FIR, the complaint, relevant correspondence or agreements, and any previous court orders.
  3. File in the Madras High Court (or the Madurai Bench where the case falls within its jurisdiction), with an affidavit and vakalatnama.
  4. Seek interim relief if there is urgency, such as a direction that no coercive steps be taken against the petitioner while the petition is pending.

What happens at the hearing

  • The court issues notice to the State, through the Public Prosecutor, and to the de facto complainant.
  • The State files a status report on the investigation. The court may ask for the case diary to see whether the investigation is genuine.
  • The court hears both sides on whether the allegations disclose a cognizable offence and whether the High Court should intervene.
  • The court may dismiss the petition, quash the FIR, or dispose of it with directions, such as allowing the investigation to continue, but directing the police to follow a particular procedure.

What the court usually does not do

The High Court does not conduct a mini-trial. It does not weigh evidence or decide disputed facts at this stage. It also hesitates to stop an investigation into a serious offence, so the strength of the petition lies in showing, on the face of the FIR and the admitted documents, that no offence is made out.

Time and cost

There is no fixed timeline. The time depends on the court's list, whether interim relief is granted and whether the State files its status report on time. Fees are agreed with your advocate. See the separate note on how fee agreements and Bar Council rules apply.

Practical tips

  • Move early. Delay can reduce the force of a petition, and arrest may happen in the meantime.
  • Be accurate and complete. Suppression of earlier proceedings can lead to dismissal and costs.
  • Cooperate with the investigation while the petition is pending, unless the court orders otherwise.
  • Keep the documents ready that show the dispute is civil in nature.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quashing petition the same as anticipatory bail?

No. Anticipatory bail protects you from arrest. Quashing seeks to end the case itself. They can be filed together.

Can I file the petition myself?

It is a technical proceeding, and advocates normally handle it.

What does "no coercive steps" mean?

It is an interim direction that the police must not arrest or take harsh action while the petition is pending.

Can the complainant oppose?

Yes. The complainant is heard and may point out why the matter should proceed.

What if the petition is dismissed?

You may appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave, or pursue other remedies such as bail and discharge.

title: Legal Costs and Free Legal Aid in a Rape Case: What Survivors and Accused Should Know
seoTitle: Legal Costs and Free Legal Aid in a Rape Case – Survivors and Accused
description: How legal fees work in a rape case, free legal aid for survivors and accused persons, victim compensation and what to ask before engaging an advocate.
html:
Money should not stand in the way of a person in a rape case, whether they are a survivor or an accused. Indian law provides free legal aid and victim compensation, and a private advocate's fee is a matter of agreement. This page explains how costs and aid work. It does not quote any fees, because they differ from advocate to advocate and case to case.

For survivors

  • Free legal aid. Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, women and children are entitled to free legal services irrespective of their income. A survivor can apply to the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in Chennai or ask the police or the Magistrate to arrange a lawyer.
  • Support during the case. Police stations and courts are expected to inform a survivor of the right to a legal aid advocate. Many One Stop Centres provide counselling and referral.
  • Compensation. The victim compensation scheme (Section 396 of the BNSS, earlier Section 357A CrPC) and the State's scheme for victims of sexual offences provide interim and final compensation, which is decided by the legal services authority or the court, and does not depend on the outcome of the trial.
  • Privacy. Hearings are held in camera, and publishing the identity of the survivor is an offence.
  • Private counsel. A survivor can also engage a private lawyer, and in many cases a victim's advocate can assist the prosecutor with the court's permission.

For a person accused

An accused is also entitled to a lawyer. The Constitution (Article 39A) and the Legal Services Authorities Act provide free legal aid for those who cannot afford one. If the accused is in custody and unrepresented, the Magistrate must inform them of the right to a legal aid advocate, and the court appoints one if the accused is not represented at trial. The legal aid advocate must give the same care as a private one.

If you engage a private advocate

  • Written agreement. Ask for the fee and scope in writing: what the fee covers (bail, trial, appeal), and what is extra.
  • Receipts. Take a receipt for each payment.
  • No promises. The Bar Council of India's rules prohibit an advocate from guaranteeing a result or charging a fee contingent on the outcome.
  • Expenses. Clarify who bears the expenses for certified copies, travel and experts.
  • Sensitivity. In these cases, how the advocate treats the person is important. Ask how they will handle the survivor's evidence respectfully, or how they will explain the process to the accused and family.

Factors that make costs higher or lower

  • Stage: bail, trial before the Sessions or Mahila Court, or appeal.
  • Complexity: number of witnesses, medical and forensic evidence, and connected proceedings.
  • Court and place: appearances at the High Court or outside Chennai.
  • Duration: how many hearings the trial requires.
  • Related cases, such as POCSO proceedings or a petition to quash.

Where to seek help in Chennai

  • Tamil Nadu State Legal Services Authority and DLSA, Chennai: free legal aid.
  • Police emergency number 112 and the Women Helpline 181.
  • CHILDLINE 1098 for children.
  • One Stop Centres and the District Social Welfare office for counselling and shelter.

Frequently asked questions

Do survivors have to pay a fee to file a complaint?

No. Registering an FIR is free, and a survivor has the right to a copy of the FIR.

Is a legal aid advocate less capable?

Legal aid advocates are enrolled lawyers who are required to represent their clients diligently. A person who is dissatisfied can ask the authority for a change.

Can an accused get legal aid?

Yes, if they cannot afford a lawyer, and the court must ensure representation at trial.

Is compensation paid only if the accused is convicted?

No. In many cases interim compensation can be granted at an early stage, and it does not depend on conviction.

Can I change my advocate midway?

Yes, but settle the fee and take back your documents, and inform the court with a fresh vakalatnama.

description: How to approach a Chennai police station: filing a complaint, FIR vs CSR, what to do if police refuse, and your rights if you are called in.
html:
People in Chennai search for individual police stations when they need to file a complaint, check on a case or support a family member who has been called in. The stations that appear most often in these searches include T15 SRMC, E3 Teynampet, T7 Tank Factory, C2 Elephant Gate, H7 Peripheral Hospital, R10 MGR Nagar, S11 Tambaram, K7 ICF, P6 Kodungaiyur, M4 Redhills, K4 Anna Nagar, J1 Saidapet, R5 Virugambakkam and M7 Manali New Town. The process and your rights are largely the same at every station, and this page explains them.

The station's address, telephone number and jurisdiction change from time to time, so this page does not list them. For the exact details of a station, check the official Greater Chennai Police website or the Kaaval Uthavi app, or call the emergency number 112.

Which station has jurisdiction?

Each station covers a defined area. A complaint is normally made at the station where the incident took place. If you are unsure, you can approach any station: a Zero FIR can be registered at any police station for a cognizable offence and then transferred to the station with jurisdiction (Section 173 of the BNSS).

Filing a complaint

  1. Write the complaint with your name, address and phone number, the date, time and place of the incident, a clear description, and the names of the persons involved, if known.
  2. Sign it and keep a copy. Ask the station to stamp and acknowledge your copy.
  3. Cognizable offence. For offences such as theft, assault, cheating or serious crimes, the police must register an FIR. The Supreme Court held in Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh (2014) that registration is mandatory, with a limited preliminary enquiry in specified categories.
  4. Other complaints. For less serious matters or disputes, the station may enter the petition in the Community Service Register (CSR) and give you a receipt. A CSR is an acknowledgement, not an FIR.
  5. Online options. Complaints can also be made through the Tamil Nadu Police citizen services portal and the Kaaval Uthavi app, depending on the type of complaint.

If the station does not register your FIR

  • Write to senior officers. Send the complaint to the Deputy Commissioner or the Commissioner of Police with a copy of the receipt. Section 173(4) of the BNSS allows you to approach the Superintendent of Police.
  • Approach the Magistrate. Under Section 175(3) of the BNSS, you can apply to the Magistrate, with an affidavit, to direct the police to register the FIR and investigate.
  • High Court. In appropriate cases, a petition can be filed in the Madras High Court.

If you or a family member are called to a police station

  • Ask for the reason in writing. For offences with imprisonment up to seven years, the police are expected to issue a notice of appearance instead of arresting automatically.
  • You have a right to know the grounds of arrest and to have a relative or friend informed.
  • You have the right to consult a lawyer (Article 22(1) of the Constitution), including during questioning.
  • Production before a Magistrate is required within twenty-four hours of arrest.
  • Medical examination can be requested, and any injury or ill-treatment should be reported to the Magistrate.
  • The D.K. Basu guidelines (Supreme Court, 1997) require an arrest memo with the arrestee's signature, a witness to the arrest and intimation to a family member.
  • Women, children and some other persons cannot ordinarily be required to attend a police station for questioning; the police should question them at their residence. A woman should not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, except in exceptional cases with a Magistrate's prior permission.

When a lawyer can help at a station

A lawyer can accompany you to the station, check that the procedure is followed, review the FIR, apply for anticipatory or regular bail and file representations to senior officers. They cannot guarantee how the police will act, and you should not pay money to anyone at a station for the registration of a case or for release.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between an FIR and a CSR?

An FIR starts a criminal investigation for a cognizable offence. A CSR receipt only records that a petition was received and enquired into.

Can I file a complaint at any police station in Chennai?

You can approach any station, and a Zero FIR can be registered for a cognizable offence. It will then be transferred to the correct station.

Do I have to pay anything to register a complaint?

No. Registration of an FIR is free, and you are entitled to a free copy.

Can the police detain me without informing my family?

No. The police must inform a relative or friend of your arrest and the place of detention.

How do I find the contact details of a station?

Use the official Greater Chennai Police website or the Kaaval Uthavi app, or call 112 for emergencies.
